tur65-0: Teeth clenching and grinding (bruxism) is when the chewing muscles work more than necessary during sleep or during the day. It affects roughly one in four or five people worldwide, and most people do not notice it. Its effects are not limited to the teeth: the jaw joint, neck muscles, sleep and headaches can also be affected. We also explain its link with neck pain separately. In this guide we explain bruxism from start to finish, like a lesson.
tur65-1: Three key points for neck pain
tur65-3: Stress and anxiety appear to be linked especially with daytime clenching; they can also increase muscle tension and sensitivity to pain. So if neck pain does not settle, the psychological load should also be asked about (psychological factors).
tur65-4: The splint given by the dentist may protect the teeth and tooth enamel against wear; however, there is not enough evidence that it reduces clenching. As long as clenching continues, the load on the jaw joint and neck muscles may continue (splint).
tur65-5: It reduces the strength of the chewing and temple muscles it is injected into. In a study using sleep tests, the frequency of clenching episodes did not change; it also does not directly address the neck muscles (what does it affect and what not?).
tur65-6: For other causes of neck pain, exercises and warning signs, you can see the neck pain guide.
tur65-7: The splint may protect the teeth and tooth enamel against wear.
tur65-8: In short: The splint given by the dentist may reduce the damage to tooth enamel. It has not been shown to stop clenching itself; so the effect on the jaw joint and neck muscles may continue. Even if you wear a splint, the causes of clenching (stress, sleep, habits) need to be addressed separately.
tur65-9: Botulinum toxin: what does it affect and what not?
tur65-10: Botulinum toxin is being used more and more for teeth clenching; so it is important to know what it changes and what it does not.
tur65-12: In the muscle it is injected into, it temporarily blocks the release of the substance that carries the contraction signal from nerve to muscle (acetylcholine); the muscle weakens and its contraction strength decreases. In a small study of 20 people assessed with sleep tests (there was no placebo group; follow-up was 4 weeks), the injection reduced the intensity of contractions in the injected muscles.
tur65-14: In the same study, the frequency and duration of clenching episodes during sleep did not change. According to the authors, the injection reduces the intensity of contraction rather than its generation. Even so, most participants reported less morning jaw stiffness after 4 weeks. Bruxism is thought to be regulated largely by the central nervous system, whereas the injection only affects the muscle it is given into. This is why factors such as stress and sleep need to be addressed separately.
tur65-15: Its effect is not permanent; it fades and disappears within a few months. The injection needs to be repeated for the effect to continue.
tur65-17: In one review, pain and bruising at the injection site, mostly temporary chewing weakness, dry mouth, difficulty swallowing and speaking, mild asymmetry of the lower face and changes in the smile were reported; these problems usually resolved within 1–4 weeks, while chewing difficulty sometimes lasted up to 12 weeks.
tur65-19: An injection into the chewing and temple muscles does not directly address the neck muscles or posture. If there is also neck pain, exercise and physiotherapy are planned separately.
tur65-20: Botulinum toxin is an injection given only by physicians, and for teeth clenching it is injected into the chewing muscle and the temple muscle. In a 2025 overview of 14 systematic reviews, a reduction in pain was reported in 10 reviews, a reduction in clenching episodes in 7 and a reduction in maximum bite force in 5. However, all the reviews had low or critically low reliability, and no firm conclusion could be drawn. In a small study of 20 people using sleep tests, on the other hand, the frequency of clenching episodes did not change while the intensity of contractions decreased; in other words, the injection may mainly affect the strength of the muscle. Its effect lasts a few months. Your physician will decide whether it is suitable.
tur65-21: Shim YJ, Lee MK, Kato T, Park HU, Heo K, Kim ST. Effects of botulinum toxin on jaw motor events during sleep in sleep bruxism patients: a polysomnographic evaluation. J Clin Sleep Med. 2014.
tur65-23: Clenching and grinding the teeth during the day or in sleep (bruxism): the neck muscles may also tighten while clenching (details below)
tur65-25: One factor that may be overlooked in neck pain that will not settle is teeth clenching and grinding (bruxism). When you clench your teeth, it is not only the jaw muscles that work: in a muscle activity study in healthy people, the activity of the front neck muscles increased markedly during the strongest clenching. In a 2026 meta-analysis of nine studies, people with neck pain were also about 3.6 times more likely to have a jaw joint problem (very low certainty of evidence). However, this review looked at jaw joint problems, not clenching; it found no study of how often clenching occurs in people with neck pain.
tur65-26: One possible explanation lies in the nervous system: in a group of nerve cells called the trigeminocervical complex, nerves carrying pain signals from the head and nerves from the upper neck converge on the same nerve cells. This convergence is thought to contribute to pain spreading between the head and neck.
tur65-27: During the years I worked with Cihan Hoca (Prof. Dr. Cihan Aksoy), we saw teeth clenching in many of the patients who came to us with neck pain that had not resolved despite previous treatments. When waking up tired, morning headaches, jaw tiredness or tooth marks on the tongue come with it, we also ask about teeth clenching. I share this as my own observation, not as a research finding; not everyone may respond in the same way.
tur65-28: Daytime clenching in particular appears to be associated with psychosocial factors. In a systematic review, people with stress were about twice as likely to have bruxism (low certainty of evidence). Stress and anxiety can also increase muscle tension and sensitivity to pain.

tur65-30: The night splint given by the dentist may protect the teeth and tooth enamel against wear. However, there is not enough evidence that the splint reduces clenching; as long as clenching continues, the load on the jaw joint and neck muscles may continue.
tur65-31: Weakens the muscle, does not stop clenching
tur65-32: The injection a physician gives into the chewing and temple muscles reduces the contraction strength of these muscles for a few months. In a small study of 20 people using sleep tests, the frequency of clenching episodes did not change, while the intensity of contractions decreased. The injection does not directly address the neck muscles.
tur65-33: If your neck pain comes with waking up tired, morning headaches, jaw pain or tiredness, or tooth marks on the tongue, you can tell your dentist and physiotherapist. For symptoms, signs and jaw exercises: Teeth clenching and grinding (bruxism) guide →
tur65-34: Is teeth clenching linked with neck pain?
tur65-35: It may be, but direct evidence is limited. In healthy people, the front neck muscles have been shown to tighten as well during the strongest clenching; jaw joint problems are also more common in people with neck pain (very low certainty of evidence). However, a 2026 review found no study directly examining how often clenching occurs in people with neck pain. The splint given by the dentist may protect the teeth but has not been shown to reduce clenching; in a study using sleep tests, botulinum toxin injected into the chewing muscle reduced the intensity of contractions but did not change their frequency. Details are in our teeth clenching guide.
